title: Chile turns its strengths -stability and growth- into new investment opportunities
summary: Chile is one of Banco Santander’s strongest markets, where it’s been a leading bank for decades and the highest rated over the past five years.
body_markdown:
Chile is one of Banco Santander’s strongest markets, where it’s been a leading bank for decades and the highest rated over the past five years. This Andean country’s vast growth potential comes from natural resources, institutional stability, and a first-class business fabric. The opportunities and challenges of Chile’s economy took centre stage at the second ever[Chile Day](https://chileday.cl/) , a Madrid-based event to showcase the country’s strengths to foreign investors.


Banco Santander is Chile’s leading bank, with over 4.5 million customers and 10% growth year on year. It holds Chile’s largest loan portfolio, with 40 billion euros granted. What’s more, Santander has some 30 billion euros in deposits there. Santander Chile is the leading bank in retail credit, with market shares of 24.6% in consumer loans and 20.9% in mortgages.


Santander has consistently proven its commitment to Chile since arriving in 1978. This year, it acquired Santander Rentas Vitalicias, a pensions company with over 4 billion euros in assets.


Chile has significant strengths: strategic resources, openness to the world and robust institutions. The opportunity lies in transforming these advantages into investment, growth and employment, with technology and Artificial Intelligence playing a key role in boosting productivity. As an investor in Chile for decades, Santander knows that the country has everything it needs to make this a reality, and we will continue to invest in its future


Ana Botín, Executive Chair of Banco Santander


The bank is also demonstrating the potential of Chile’s economy through other initiatives, such as the announcement of an 800-million-dollar investment over the next three years. This figure includes the acquisition of the pensions business, as well as projects to ramp up technology transformation, revamp the branch network, and make headway with its new headquarters,[Campus Santander.](https://banco.santander.cl/campus-santander) This investment will enable Santander to delve deeper into the use of technology, data and artificial intelligence to enhance customer experience, simplify processes, and boost its capacity to respond.


In addition, the bank will invest in its branches under a strategy that combines digital services with in-person care at WorkCafés, an innovative take on traditional branches. They provide customers and non-customers with financial services, co-working areas and meeting rooms free of charge, and specialty coffee. As the brainchild of Santander Chile in 2016, there are now 250 WorkCafés in eight of the Group’s markets: Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Mexico, Portugal, Spain, the UK, and the US.


Against this backdrop, Andrés Trautmann, CEO and Country Head of Santander Chile, highlighted the country’s “resources, talent, and abilities. Our challenge is to use them positively through partnerships, long-term norms, and inclusion”.


**Opportunity knocks**


Banco Santander Executive Chair Ana Botín took part in Chile Day by sharing the bank’s vision of the market in an interview with Chilean reporter Mónica Pérez Marín. According to Botín, "those of us who understand Chile well invest here. Santander’s success story in the country demonstrates that sound long-term investments can be made in Chile. Chile has everything it needs to enjoy many years of further growth ahead”.


Chile arrives at Chile Day Madrid 2026 with substantial confidence from outside the country. In 2025, it received 14.513 billion dollars in foreign direct investment, up 10.8% on the previous year. Reinvestment of profits accounted for the lion’s share, which shows how overseas-based companies continue to commit to Chile. Add to that a portfolio of 95.149 billion dollars for 2026-2030, which will be primarily private and boast a significant share of foreign capital.


The main challenge will be to strengthen competitiveness and turn Chile’s potential into investment and growth. Investment in energy is expected to reach over 20 billion dollars by 2030, with key projects such as the HVDC Kimal-Lo Aguirre transmission line (1.275 billion dollars), Volta I hydrogen and green ammonia project (1.235 billion dollars), and the Cabo Negro carbon neutral power station (808 million dollars).


Moreover, Chile’s attractiveness also comes from other sectors. The InvestChile portfolio accounts for over 5.6 billion dollars in global, technology and data centre services, not to mention a further 5.572 billion dollars in infrastructure and concessions. And the capital market reform seeks to ease access for international investors and bolster the financing of smaller-cap enterprises.
